newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea names new farm minister in power shift.
newsitem.headline: North Korea names new farm minister in power shift.

text.p: North Korea, battling to recover from two years of devastating floods, on Tuesday named a new farm minister in the latest of many recent changes to the communist country's power structure.

A broadcast by the North's official Korean Central Radio, monitored in Tokyo, referred to Han Ik-hyon, an obscure regional farm committee chairman, as chairman of the State Agricultural Commission, or farm minister.

While it was the first time he had been identified as having the job, the radio did not say when Han took over from Kim Won-jin, who had been farm minister since 1990 and was last mentioned by North Korea's official media 10 months ago.
Han's new title was revealed in a list of dignitaries attending an official function, said Tokyo-based Radiopress, which monitors North Korea's state-run media.
Han, whose age was not given, was neither a member nor alternate member of the several hundred-strong central committee that rules the reclusive Stalinist nation.
Radiopress analysts speculated Kim may have been sacked for his failure to get the country's agricultural production back on course after floods in 1995 and 1996 caused near famine.

They said North Korean leader Kim Jong-il's decision to elevate Han, a little-known provincial official, to the top post in restoring agricultural production was an indication that he had lost patience with the efforts of veteran bureaucrats.
"There are two angles to the news of today's cabinet change," said Noriyuki Suzuki, a North Korean analyst at Radiopress.
"The first is that it is part of the ongoing leadership change in the Pyongyang hierarchy and the second is that it is part of a reshuffle in the agricultural establishment."
Han's elevation to a cabinet post follows a month of drastic changes in North Korea's leadership.
On February 12, the country's ideology chief Hwang Jang-yop defected to the South Korean diplomatic mission in Beijing.

Hwang is still holed up in Beijing. His defection was soon followed by the appointment of a new prime minister, Hong Song-nam, to replace Kang Son-san, a powerful politician once ranked sixth in the hierarchy.
Then North Korea reported that Defence Minister Choe Kwang and Deputy Defence Minister Kim Kwang-jin had died within a week of each other.
The leadership changes have been played out against the background of a nation in crisis struggling to survive flood waters which washed away crops, land, roads and bridges

In a sign of the North's plight, Pyongyang has requested food aid from the United States, China and other countries and the issue is now linked to Pyongyang's possible participation in talks to sign a peace treaty formally ending the 1950-1953 Korean War.
The Korean War ended with only an armistice, not a full-fledged peace treaty, and the two Koreas technically remain at war.

In January, the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), an arm of the United Nations, said food shortages in North Korea were likely to worsen considerably this year and require large-scale international assistance to ensure minimum needs are met.
"Two successive years of floods have undoubtedly set back agriculture and significantly compounded underlying food production problems in the country," an FAO report said.
